title: Canonical direct rotation
subtitle: G2 lecture 049000 · expanded mathematical companion
adaptation: Standalone companion adapted from the source spoken lecture and display-only mathematics appendix. Explicit hypotheses, stepwise proofs, worked examples, and local vector diagrams; no narration edits.

slides.title: Which unitary is the direct rotation?
slides.lead: Many unitaries carry one subspace onto another; positivity chooses the canonical shorter transport.
body: Even for two lines, turning through θ and turning through θ+π both map the first line onto the second. The direct rotation is the choice that rotates the principal planes by their acute angles.
For general closed subspaces, this choice is encoded by a polar factor built from their orthogonal projections. The construction avoids arbitrary rotations within repeated-angle eigenspaces.
slides.takeaway: Direct rotation selects a canonical unitary among many possible subspace transports.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Which unitary is the direct rotation?

slides.title: Two lines and a sign choice
slides.lead: Let U be horizontal and let V be tilted counterclockwise by 0<θ<π/2.
body: The shorter planar rotation R(θ) carries the unit vector e to v with ⟨e,v⟩=cos θ>0. A rotation through θ+π sends e to −v and produces the negative cosine.
A positive diagonal compression distinguishes these two choices even though they map the same unoriented line onto V. In higher dimensions the same test is applied to both diagonal blocks.
slides.takeaway: Positive cosine blocks encode the shorter turn.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Two lines and a sign choice

slides.title: The canonical projection formula
body: On a principal plane K equals cos θ times R(θ). If the projection gap is below one, C has a bounded inverse and the direct rotation is W=KC^{-1}.
This formula makes W a unitary intertwiner from P to Q. It also specifies the action on the complementary side, not merely on the selected subspace U.
slides.takeaway: The canonical unitary is the polar factor of the projection-based intertwiner.

slides.title: Acute pairs without a bounded cosine inverse
slides.lead: The crossed defects vanish when U∩V⊥=0 and U⊥∩V=0.
body: In this case K and K* have zero kernels. Polar decomposition K=WC gives an isometry W with dense range, so W is onto and hence unitary.
No numerical bound C≥cI is needed for this existence argument. Infinite sequences of angles can approach ninety degrees while W remains well defined as a unitary polar factor.
slides.takeaway: The polar factor exists even when the cosine has no bounded inverse.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Acute pairs without a bounded cosine inverse

slides.title: Characterize the correct unitary
slides.lead: An arbitrary intertwining unitary T can rotate within U or U⊥ and still satisfy TP=QT.
body: Require both diagonal compressions PTP and (I−P)T(I−P) to be positive self-adjoint operators. For the direct rotation, those blocks are cosine operators on the corresponding source halves.
The positivity condition rules out the negative-cosine choice from the planar example. It is a genuine operator condition, not merely the sign of one scalar inner product.
slides.takeaway: Positivity of both diagonal blocks singles out the shorter transport.

slides.title: Why this direct rotation is unique
slides.lead: Suppose T is unitary, TP=QT, and both diagonal compressions are positive.
body: Set B=PTP+(I−P)T(I−P). Intertwining lets us rewrite K=TB. Since T is unitary, K*K=B²; positivity forces B=|K|=C.
Thus K=TC. If the crossed defects vanish, the polar factor of K is unique on the dense support, so T=W. This is the central uniqueness argument.
slides.takeaway: Positive compression identifies the modulus and forces the canonical polar factor.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Why this direct rotation is unique

slides.title: Two reflections make twice the angle
slides.lead: The reflection through a subspace U is J_U=2P−I, and similarly for V.
body: On a principal plane, J_V J_U rotates through 2θ. The direct rotation W is the half-angle motion, so W²=J_V J_U.
The product of two reflections therefore reconstructs a rotation, while the positivity choice selects the preferred square root. The order of the two reflections fixes the orientation.
slides.takeaway: Direct rotation is the principal half-turn of the reflection product.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Two reflections make twice the angle

slides.title: Why the square-root branch matters
slides.lead: In a uniformly acute complex Hilbert-space pair, the spectrum of J_VJ_U avoids the negative real branch point −1.
body: Continuous functional calculus can then choose the principal square root of the unitary reflection product. That root agrees with the canonical direct rotation on each principal plane.
At a right-angle block the reflection product is −I, which admits opposite square roots. The canonical branch cannot be continued across that obstruction without further choices.
slides.takeaway: The branch cut reflects genuine geometric ambiguity at a right angle.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Why the square-root branch matters

slides.title: Swapping source and target
slides.lead: A canonical transport should undo itself when the pair of subspaces is reversed.
body: Switching P and Q replaces K by its adjoint K*. Its polar factor is therefore the adjoint W* of the original direct rotation.
This agrees with principal-plane geometry: if W rotates forward through θ, the reversed map rotates through −θ. The construction is compatible with both forward and backward transport.
slides.takeaway: The reversed direct rotation is the inverse of the original.

slides.title: Recover the transport from the projections
slides.lead: The proof rests on three ingredients: projection identities, polar decomposition, and positivity.
body: Derive K*K=I−(P−Q)², take its positive square root C, and obtain W as the polar factor of K. Verify WP=QW and the positivity of both diagonal compressions.
On a principal plane, compute the reflection product and see explicitly why its half-angle is the positive-cosine choice. Together these facts characterize the direct rotation.
slides.takeaway: The construction is intrinsic and its uniqueness follows from the positive polar factor.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 049000 · Recover the transport from the projections
